j.learned_fact: Winds carry millions of tons of Saharan dust across the Atlantic each year, and the phosphorus in it fertilizes the phosphorus-poor soils of the Amazon.
j.thinking_skill: Counterfactual testing: removing one input (Saharan phosphorus) from a nutrient-balance model to see whether the system still holds
j.notes: Prose and sentence structure read as middle-school, below a 16-year-old's level, and the 'model' Colton builds in an evening is hand-waved ('the numbers collapsed'). The teacher's closing 'that's how scientists actually work' is a bolted-on moral; 'lavish complexity' is a forced word choice.

j.learned_fact: Children grow while they sleep, and a steady bedtime routine (bath, book, lights out) helps sleep come fast and last all night.
j.thinking_skill: Measuring change against a fixed landmark (comparing his head to the branch he stood under in fall)
j.notes: Growth is compressed so that a few nights of good sleep read as the cause of a visible height gain; the causal link between the bedtime routine and heading the ball is looser than the story implies. The 'First, Next, Then, Last' sequence is slightly formulaic.

j.learned_fact: Spreading the same number of study hours over many days produces better retention than concentrating them in a few long sessions (the spacing effect).
j.thinking_skill: Distinguishing a testable explanation from an unfalsifiable one ('she's just smart') and holding hours constant to compare study schedules
j.notes: Alicia's evidence is anecdotal (two cousins, her own French words) and she admits it proves nothing, so the reader gets the idea without any stated research; the rowing parallel is elegant but the pacing analogy is not the same mechanism as spacing. Very strong prose, arguably a shade above a 15-year-old.

j.learned_fact: A pinhole in a box projects an upside-down image of the scene outside. FALSE/contradictory: the story then claims the analogy is 'high things went high, low things went low', which is the opposite of the inverted image it just described.
j.thinking_skill: Analogical reasoning (mapping the pinhole image onto staff position), though the analogy does not hold
j.notes: A pinhole-camera demonstration in a drumming lesson makes no sense, and the 'click' Zachary has contradicts the inversion the story itself states. Two unrelated prompts glued together; the drum notation is never actually explained.

j.learned_fact: A hiccup is a sudden spasm of the diaphragm; eating quickly and drinking soda before playing can trigger them, and slow controlled breathing can stop them.
j.thinking_skill: Tracking when a symptom occurs, forming a trigger hypothesis and testing a remedy across several sessions
j.notes: The braces/appearance thread is set up and then dismissed with a non-sequitur ('It wasn't about his braces... at all'). 'Credible performance' misuses 'credible' (meant 'creditable'); 'cooperate' is forced. The confidence lesson is stated rather than earned.

j.learned_fact: A pulley is a wheel at the top of a flagpole: pulling down on one end of the rope makes the other end (and the flag) go up.
j.thinking_skill: Observing a real mechanism and reproducing its parts in the right order in a drawing
j.notes: The 'First, Next, Then, Last' painting sequence is a visible scaffold, and the basement-juice detour is filler. Otherwise a clean, age-appropriate observation story.

j.learned_fact: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees, so knowing 45 and 90 lets you predict the third is 45 before measuring it with a protractor.
j.thinking_skill: Deductive prediction: computing a value from a rule and then verifying it by measurement
j.notes: The teacher's framing 'the kite should fly straight, so every triangle must add up to 180' is a false causal link (the angle sum holds regardless), and the 'bent corner' fix is never coherent. Dialogue is stilted ('Your effort on your first day shows real thinking'); the rule is delivered as a classroom lecture.

j.learned_fact: A seed sends its root down first and its shoot up toward the light, even if the seed was planted upside down.
j.thinking_skill: Making a prediction (plant will grow into the floor), observing, and revising it
j.notes: The monkey drawing and the S-E-E-D spelling are bolted-on early-literacy beats unrelated to the plot. Short and effective otherwise.

j.learned_fact: GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast relative to ground clocks; without a relativistic correction, position errors would grow by kilometers per day, and a receiver needs at least four satellites. Minor inaccuracy: the gravitational part of the correction comes from general relativity (1915), not the 1905 equations.
j.thinking_skill: Analogical reasoning between reading error messages backward and layered systems where every hidden layer must be right
j.notes: Three vocabulary words are misused: 'encumbrance' for a bug, 'incipient' for a basic demo, and 'sequester real GPS data' for obtaining it. The GPS material arrives as a summarized article rather than through the plot, and the hiking-glitch thread is left unresolved.

j.learned_fact: Young children have twenty baby teeth; they start getting loose around age six and bigger teeth grow in.
j.thinking_skill: Counting to twenty and relating a future event (loose teeth) to age
j.notes: The melting ice-pop paragraph is filler with no connection to the plot. Theo's 'brush so they'll be ready' is charming but implies brushing hastens adult teeth.

j.learned_fact: When your currency weakens, the same foreign-priced item costs more in your money, while your own goods become cheaper for foreign buyers, so importers/travelers lose and exporters gain.
j.thinking_skill: Isolating a variable (re-pricing in euros to separate the flight's price from the exchange rate) and reasoning about the reciprocal effect on exporters
j.notes: The words 'exchange rate' and 'depreciation' never appear, so a 15-year-old learns the mechanism without the name to look it up. Register is slightly young for 9th grade; otherwise excellent.

j.learned_fact: Teenagers' biological sleep clocks shift later than younger children's or adults', so not being able to fall asleep early is physiology, not laziness.
j.thinking_skill: Forming a hypothesis from a pattern of evidence and designing a simple test (no alarm, note natural wake time)
j.notes: One alarm-free morning cannot distinguish a shifted clock from ordinary sleep debt, yet the story treats it as proof. Maya at 12 is a little young for the classic circadian shift, and 'cajoling' is a forced word.

j.learned_fact: A seed's root grows down and its shoot grows up toward light even when the seed is planted upside down.
j.thinking_skill: Recalling a rule and checking it against an observation
j.notes: Contradictory: Ella plants the seed upside down on purpose while citing the lesson, then is worried it is 'the wrong way'. The dance opening is unrelated and dropped.

j.learned_fact: Lightning heats air to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, roughly five times the Sun's surface, and the air's rapid expansion makes the boom we call thunder. Muddled claim: it says distant thunder 'takes longer to reach us, so it sounds soft' (delay does not cause softness; distance does).
j.thinking_skill: Explaining a scary phenomenon by its physical mechanism to reassure a younger child
j.notes: Nicholas delivers the facts as a mini-lecture, and Maya stumbling in 'awkward and embarrassed' plus the water-tower landmark are bolted-on prompt items with no plot function.

j.learned_fact: A random sample can represent a much larger group, and the sample size needed does not depend on how big the population is, as long as the draw is random ('stir first').
j.thinking_skill: Designing a random-sampling experiment and reasoning about why randomness matters for representativeness
j.notes: The demonstration re-samples 42 slips she has already counted, so it shows sample-to-population agreement only loosely, and the 'same thousand either way' claim is asserted rather than explained. Register reads slightly young for a 9th grader.

j.learned_fact: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate and three tiny bones (hammer, anvil, stirrup) pass the vibration into the inner ear; the stirrup is about the size of a grain of rice. FALSE: ringing after a blow to the ear is not the stirrup 'still shaking'; the bones stop almost instantly and ringing comes from the inner ear/nerves.
j.thinking_skill: Sorting by two different criteria and testing a hypothesis with a controlled comparison (soft kick vs hard kick)
j.notes: The central explanation for the ringing is wrong, and the fence-clang test measures the fence, not his ear. Lively and well pitched otherwise.

j.learned_fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, so seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by distance.
j.thinking_skill: Refuting a common explanation with a counterexample and testing an alternative with a physical model
j.notes: Marcus's share-out speech ('common commerce in ideas') and Priya's 'vulnerable' line are forced vocabulary insertions that no ten-year-old would say. The story never says it is describing the Northern Hemisphere.

j.learned_fact: The first web page went online at CERN in 1991, and in 1993 Tim Berners-Lee persuaded CERN to release the web's technology royalty-free.
j.thinking_skill: Counterfactual reasoning about how the web would differ if its technology had been licensed
j.notes: The bug is technically shaky: a stray semicolon inside parentheses would not produce an 'expecting a colon' error, and the CERN paragraph conveniently 'pasted in' is a lucky find. Otherwise assured, human-sounding prose.

j.learned_fact: Simpson's paradox: aggregated data can show a trend that reverses when broken down by group. BUT the numbers do not add up: 'forty-eight percent women and fifty-two percent women' is garbled; engineering is said to have 44% women applicants and then 27 of 48 (56%); the selective programs (applied math 31/180 women) have FEW women, which is the opposite of what the paradox needs.
j.thinking_skill: Disaggregating data by group to detect a reversal between aggregate and subgroup trends
j.notes: The internal figures contradict the explanation the story reaches, so a careful reader cannot reconstruct the paradox. 'The pragmatism of a conciliatory visualization' is purple and semantically empty.

j.learned_fact: Young children have twenty baby teeth; they fall out when ready and bigger teeth grow in.
j.thinking_skill: Accepting delayed gratification after understanding a cause (the tooth comes out when ready)
j.notes: Very slight; the 'wonder' moment is a tooth that was already loose in the first paragraph. Mom's fact is stated plainly but briefly.

j.learned_fact: The first commercial cell phone in the 1980s cost nearly four thousand dollars, and the 1973 prototype used for the first cell-phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms.
j.thinking_skill: Holding two competing historical narratives at once and recognizing that memory selectively edits the past
j.notes: The tech history is a brief aside inside a comedy of school hijinks; the vending-machine 'felony' ending undercuts the reflection. Some jokes strain ('like a man defending a mansion').

j.learned_fact: Anthropologist Robin Dunbar proposed that humans can maintain roughly 150 stable relationships, so a thousand followers is a different category from friends.
j.thinking_skill: Distinguishing categories (a count versus a relationship) and historicizing one's own feelings
j.notes: 'Everyone's an acolyte at something' misuses 'acolyte' (an assistant/devotee, not a novice). The program's second part (checking messages) is described too vaguely to be believable, and the Dunbar note is delivered via a conveniently underlined library book.

j.learned_fact: Spacing study sessions over days yields better long-term memory than the same hours crammed; Ebbinghaus documented this in 1885.
j.thinking_skill: Ruling out alternative explanations (ability, motivation) before accepting the spacing explanation and checking it against research
j.notes: Forced vocabulary: 'favorite memento cookbook' is meaningless, and 'reciprocal relationship' between spacing and retention is wrong (the effect runs one way). A Celtics game at breakfast time and 'eight hours yesterday alone' for an exam that 'always came easily' are small inconsistencies.

j.learned_fact: A pinhole box safely projects an upside-down image of the Sun, so you can watch an eclipse turn into a crescent without looking at the Sun.
j.thinking_skill: Classifying items by two attributes at once (line/space and high/low)
j.notes: Two unrelated lessons share one story; the 'four piles' of notes is a contrived classification that does not actually teach note reading. The immigrant grandfather 'who built things' and the retreat indoors are bolted-on prompt items.

j.learned_fact: The value of a good depends on the situation of the person holding it: a bottle of water is worth a dollar by a store register and a silver ring on a ridge with no water.
j.thinking_skill: Untangling an emotional narrative from physical evidence and judging each claim on its own evidence
j.notes: The economics (marginal/situational value) is left implicit and unnamed, so the reader gets the intuition without the concept. Marcus diagnosing a 'clean manufacturing crack' from photos is a stretch.

j.learned_fact: GPS satellite clocks would run about 38 microseconds a day fast without relativistic correction, and errors would grow by kilometers per day; a receiver times signals from at least four satellites.
j.thinking_skill: Reasoning about correctness as a stack of layers, each of which must hold, while isolating a bug by reverting the one change she made
j.notes: 'The whole encumbrance' and 'sequester that rule somewhere' are misused; 'semi-semicolon' is nonsense. Swapping lat/lon for both points would not usually give 11,000 km (only if one point is swapped), so the bug is under-specified.

j.learned_fact: The gambler's fallacy: past streaks do not make an independent outcome 'due'. FALSE as applied: breakouts are not independent events (yesterday's skin state does predict today's), and the mother contradicts herself ('yesterday doesn't make today more or less likely' vs 'over time good habits do matter').
j.thinking_skill: Recognizing that a streak does not create a 'debt' the next outcome must repay
j.notes: A skincare lecture from Mom is a juvenile frame for a 16-year-old, and the statistics lesson is delivered as explicit exposition. 'Presentiment' (a premonition) and 'reify' are misused.

j.learned_fact: The tiny lines on fingertips are fingerprints, and no two people, not even twins, have the same ones.
j.thinking_skill: Using physical evidence to rule himself out and identify a culprit
j.notes: The fingerprint clue is never actually used to identify Kit (her frosting-covered fingers do that), so the fact is decorative. 'Lunchtime' at a hockey game and the shining ice are filler; sentences run a touch long for a 5-year-old.

j.learned_fact: Paying only a $25 minimum on a $1,000 credit-card balance takes about five and a half years and costs over $600 in interest, while paying $100 a month clears it in under a year (the figures are consistent with roughly 20% APR).
j.thinking_skill: Modeling a repayment schedule and changing one input (monthly payment) to compare long-run outcomes
j.notes: The interest rate is never stated, so a reader cannot check the arithmetic without assuming one. Priya being 18 with a robotics build costing a thousand dollars sits a little old for a 14-year-old reader, though the prose is accessible.

j.learned_fact: An empty tummy makes a growling sound, which means you are hungry; the dog's does too.
j.thinking_skill: Inferring a cause (hunger) from a bodily sensation and checking it by eating
j.notes: The dog Ben appears out of nowhere at the end, and the hot bench and knife are safety beats bolted on with no plot role. Choppy, unparagraphed text.

j.learned_fact: Regression to the mean: an unusually good or bad result is often followed by a more ordinary one, so a single drop or rebound does not prove anything changed; you need many observations over time.
j.thinking_skill: Recognizing regression to the mean and proposing longitudinal evidence to distinguish it from real change
j.notes: Alexander's own data confounds effort with luck (he did study less for the 84), so his conclusion is under-supported; the class discussion mirroring his problem is convenient. 'Improving his recovery' is garbled and the ending is a cliché.

j.learned_fact: Light bends when it passes from water to air, so a fish appears shallower and closer than it really is; you have to aim below where it seems to be.
j.thinking_skill: Analogical reasoning (refraction as 'hidden problem beneath the surface'), though the analogy is strained
j.notes: The refraction fact has no logical connection to over-salting sauce, and the cooking lesson ('trust steps you can't understand') is not what actually fixed the sauce. 'Corrosive to his tongue' misuses 'corrosive'; the fact is delivered as a dad-anecdote lecture.

j.learned_fact: The first web page went online at CERN in 1991, CERN released the technology royalty-free in 1993, and a restored copy of that first page is still online.
j.thinking_skill: Counterfactual reasoning about ownership of the web, plus catching and checking her own wish to over-generalize
j.notes: Long, and Marcus reading the fact 'off a crumpled printout' is a contrivance. 'Mendacity' and 'enthralled' are slightly ornamental. Otherwise the most complete story in the set.

j.learned_fact: Breathing is driven mainly by the diaphragm, and a hiccup is a sudden spasm of that muscle with the vocal cords snapping shut; slow deep breathing can calm it.
j.thinking_skill: Applying a remembered mechanism (diaphragm spasm) to design a remedy and testing it
j.notes: The deodorant and hiccup episodes are two hygiene prompts stitched together; 'cooperate' is forced. The remedy works instantly, which is convenient.

j.learned_fact: Some pines, such as the lodgepole pine, have cones sealed with resin that open only in the heat of a wildfire, dropping seeds onto freshly cleared ground.
j.thinking_skill: Comparing two attributes (weight vs thickness) and inferring purpose from an unusual structure
j.notes: A sealed pinecone falling out of a library book is a contrived trigger, and the book-weight sorting is a detour that goes nowhere. 'The tree was planning ahead' is teleological but excusable as child speech.

j.learned_fact: Doubling every dimension multiplies volume (and weight) by eight but cross-section (leg strength) by only four, so a scaled-up animal needs proportionally thicker legs (square-cube law). Muddled step: it says more surface area 'meant more weight', which is wrong (weight follows volume).
j.thinking_skill: Proportional scaling reasoning about how strength and weight change with size
j.notes: 'Voracious detail work' misuses 'voracious' and 'rescind her original plan' is forced. The calculation is narrated confusingly ('doubled it... multiplied by four'), the 'twice the scale' assignment becomes a three-foot ant, and the studio-object tests are hand-waved.

j.learned_fact: The brain uses about 20 percent of the body's energy while weighing only about 2 percent of it; a product is the answer when two numbers are multiplied (6 x 4 = 24). Misleading inference: the story implies hard thinking noticeably raises energy use, but the brain's share barely changes with mental effort.
j.thinking_skill: Proportional reasoning (a small thing can use a large share) and checking a hunch against a reference source
j.notes: A spelling test with a 'math section' exists only to plant the word 'product'; the hunger explanation is a common misconception dressed as discovery. Voice is otherwise lively and age-true.

j.learned_fact: The first web page went online at CERN in 1991, and in 1993 Berners-Lee persuaded CERN to release the technology royalty-free; also, a loop over ten items runs from index 0 to 9 (off-by-one error).
j.thinking_skill: Counterfactual reasoning about what a licensed web would have meant for access and learning
j.notes: The kitchen conversation is on-the-nose, and Keisha's 'he gave away his company' goes uncorrected (there was no company). 'Annuity' and 'aggrandize' are forced but used correctly.

j.learned_fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, so winter is caused by the tilt of Earth's axis: a low sun spreads its light over more ground, like a tilted flashlight, so it heats less.
j.thinking_skill: Refuting a hypothesis with data and proposing an alternative mechanism (angle of incidence) supported by an analogy
j.notes: 'He looked almost vulnerable' and the closing 'How would you paraphrase...' are forced vocabulary insertions, and the tablet conveniently confirms the tilt answer. Reads a touch young for 6th grade.

j.learned_fact: Round things roll smoothly because they have no corners; square things bump and stop.
j.thinking_skill: Comparing two outcomes and attributing the difference to a single feature (corners)
j.notes: The letters A and B on the cookies are a literacy beat with no plot role, and rolling cookies down a ramp is an odd classroom activity. Simple and clear otherwise.

j.learned_fact: The dark spot in the middle of the eye (the pupil) shrinks in bright light and grows in the dark; it is a hole that changes size.
j.thinking_skill: Controlled observation (vary the light, watch the pupil) and applying the finding to a new situation
j.notes: The coach's clue 'watch your eyes when you come inside' is cryptic, and giving his eyes 'time to get used to the light' on a cloudy day is a weak link to seeing the ball. 'First, Next, Then, Last' is a visible scaffold and 'ill' is forced.

j.learned_fact: Sound travels into the ear and makes tiny parts inside vibrate, and louder sounds make them vibrate more.
j.thinking_skill: Controlled comparison (quiet snap vs loud snap) to test a hypothesis about loudness
j.notes: The 'which sport am I better at' setup is abandoned, and the ear explanation stays vague (no eardrum, no bones named). Feeling 'something inside vibrating' from a finger snap is dubious.
